field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by KI6UGB / Jim Robison, KJ6MRV, on January 26, 2014)

Folks, I need some advice. I'm looking for a mobile antenna for my Yaesu FT-2900. I have been using 38" mag mounts and the antenna keeps hitting low trees. A 19" model would be better, but what will that do to my range? Any suggestions?

field.name: content
field.p: Hi Jim, I do have some experience with trees and antennas so here is my 2 cents.

Before you make a change, what is your mag mount mounted to? Do you have enough ground plane area to support a 1/4 wave? In my current Jeep situation, my antenna mount is essentially on the end of a mast that has virtually no ground plane area. A 1/2 wave antenna works great there, but a 1/4 wave is almost useless. So before you make the change, make sure you have enough ground plane. 1/4 wave in every direction will give decent results.

Are you still apt to hit branches with the 1/4 wave? If so, those short antennas don't bend nearly as much as the longer ones. If using a rigid NMO mount you might end up bending some sheet metal as well.

So back to your basic questions. I had very good luck with a Comet (now NGC) B-10 when it was mounted to the top of my van. It's quite short, only 12 inches, but works as both a 2m and 70cm antenna. That's the good part - the down side is there is virtually no gain to speak of, and it does need a ground plane. If I put it on my Jeep mount, it's a little better than a dummy load. I think Doug KF6LMB is using the same on top of his pickup. When I had it mounted on the van, I could hit any repeater in this area - Santa Rosa to Vacaville and Novato with 50 watts. Not nearly as far as a 1/2 wave with gain. A 1/2 wave on the same mount will get me into the Palo Alto repeater from Santa Rosa using 50 watts.
I do have a spare 1/4 wave mag mount that I won in the SCRA raffle that you are welcome to borrow as a comparison test between your 1/2 wave and a 1/4 wave before you go drilling any holes.

field.name: content
field.p: Charlie, thanks for the thinking points. I will be mounting it on my Volvo wagon, so I guess the ground plane is as big as most SUVs, though not as big as an American van. Thank you for the loan offer. I have a mag mount, I just don't know what to stick in it.

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by Doug on Earthlink, September 22, 2013)

Jim, not sure what Charlie said I had on my pickup, but it was one of those MFJ (mighty fine junk) antennas, 1/4 wave. Cost used to be 29 bucks. I seem to have good luck with it. It stands about 18 inches tall. The only bad luck I had with it was that I forgot to take it out when I went in the carwash. Oops. An example of its use: above Nice on the hill, I contacted Charlie on the old English Hill antenna in Sebastopol with 60 watts. Same story contacting Mt Diablo, from up at Loon Lake 30 miles east of Georgetown, or 50 miles east of Auburn. This may be the loaner that Charlie has to loan to you. Good luck, KF6LMB

field.name: content
field.p: Hi Jim, just a note of caution - I think that not all mag mounts will be tuned for all antennas, they have a matching coil built in to both couple to the ground plane and match the antenna. For a proper match and best results, be sure to use one designed for the antenna being used (one designed for a 5/8 wave antenna will differ from one designed for a 1/4 wave, etc.)

field.name: content
field.p: Hi Bob, this might be the case if you are using a mag mount with a non-standard interface, meaning the mag mount was intended to be no more than part of a complete antenna system, not a separate product.
But all mag mounts I've seen sold as mag mounts using standard interfaces such as SO-239 or NMO can accommodate virtually any antenna with the proper connector.

I have used NMO mounts on my vehicles (both permanent and mag mounts) and have freely interchanged between 5/8 wave and 1/4 wave antennas with no ill effects. I have 1/4 wave antennas on the permanent mounts since that allows me to put the vehicles in the garage, but if I know I'll be somewhere a little extra oomph will help, I swap in the 5/8 wave once I'm out of the garage.
The 5/8 wave antennas I've used have their loading coil in their bases, between the NMO mount and the whip.

field.name: content
field.p: Hi Jim, I'm a little late with a suggestion for a short mobile mag mount antenna, but here it goes: I have MP Antenna's "Super M Classic" tri-band mobile mag mount. This is a very well built all stainless 2m/220/440 ham band antenna with an overall height of 19". It handles 200 watts, and works especially well in town and in the hills due to its quasi-circular polarization. You can see it in Universal Radio's catalog, or online from other sellers.

field.name: content
field.p: Thank you for all the great suggestions. I have decided to buy a Tram 1185. I like the short 19 inch height, the wide 3 inch base, and I especially like the $16 price.

field.name: content
field.p: I am not sure you will be happy with it, Jim. Why? Because it has no gain on two meters and, I am only guessing here, you get what you pay for. There is little to be said for it on eham.net. Personally, I would choose something else. No 19" whip (1/4 wave) is going to give you gain. I am assuming that you are primarily interested in two meter operation.

field.name: content
field.p: Hi Jim, I use a 19 inch whip on a NMO threaded mag mount on my SUV because it fits inside my garage. John is correct that the quarter wave antenna will not give you gain in excess of a quarter wavelength ground plane radiator. That may be entirely satisfactory for most purposes. When I need gain, I swap a longer half-wavelength antenna for the quarter wave ground plane, and get somewhat greater range. While you get what you pay for, what you pay for may be entirely adequate for your purposes.

field.name: content
field.p: My theory is that I'll get better results with a 1/4 wave mounted on the roof than a 1/2 wave being dragged behind the car after it hits a low tree limb, or missing entirely after the whip got knocked out of the mount.

field.name: content
field.p: Hi all, ditto to Jim Robison's remark. My Diamond NR770HAB mounted off the back of my Rav4 has survived all the oak trees and parking garages for 2+ years now. Better longevity than anything else I've used. It also has a fold-over which is fine when I remember it.

field.name: content
field.p: Fred / John, this question interested me enough that I tried some research. I spoke with Powerwerx and they also have no standard. However, I took a look at the solar power world and found something interesting: in solar controllers, they use red as the baseline battery connector color, and on the solar array side (multiple voltages) they use yellow as the standard connector color. Yellow is enough of a difference in color to make you at least question the voltage if nothing else.

field.name: content
field.p: Share your tips and tricks here.

Need a way to carry and dispense paracord without it kinking? Take a 1.25 liter plastic soft drink bottle, wash and dry it, then drill a 3/32 hole in the cap (deburr it). Feed 100 feet of unrolled paracord into the bottle, rattling it to push the cord to the bottom. Thread the loose end through the cap for storage in your trunk. Not as fast as using a reel, but it stores nicely and keeps the cord clean.

field.name: content
field.p: Tip for winding wire antennas for storage: use a kite reel (available on Amazon for under $10). Remove the kite twine and cut a notch where it guides onto the spool, then drill a hole in the reel to feed wire onto it. The kite reel's folding handle and ratchet stop make it convenient. 75 feet of End Fed antenna wire wound on the reel stores well - this method keeps wire smooth without kinking, and works well for portable radial wires too.

field.name: content
field.p: Undocumented FTM-400 feature - Cross Band Repeat. Yaesu left this out of the user manual, but the radio actually supports it.

Entering cross-band mode: Turn the APRS modem off. Set a UHF frequency in either the upper or lower display (VFO or memory). Set a VHF frequency in the other display (VFO or memory). Turn the FTM-400 off. Press and hold the lower 3 buttons to the right of the display, then press the power button. "X-BAND Repeater" will show between the upper and lower frequency displays if it worked.

Exiting cross-band mode: Turn the FTM-400 off. Press and hold the lower 3 buttons to the right of the display, then press the power button again. "X-BAND Repeater" will no longer be displayed. Return the frequencies to your preferences, and turn the APRS modem back on if you run APRS.

field.name: content
field.p: A newly licensed ham with an electrical engineering background asks about grounding requirements for a home station, wondering whether extensive grounding measures are needed given how rare lightning is in the area. Describes the standard recommendation: an 8-foot ground rod connected to all equipment via copper piping, lightning arrestors on antennas, and a bond to the home's electrical ground.

field.name: content
field.p: Uses a grounding bus tied to a half-inch copper braided strap connected to a ground rod (limited to 4 feet by soil conditions). Relies on disconnecting equipment during storms rather than lightning protection, and recommends Joe K6AWA, who gave a good grounding presentation at the club.

field.name: content
field.p: Installed an 8-foot ground rod with a random wire antenna routed through a lightning arrestor. The rod connects to the foundation rebar, with plans to run about 100 feet of #6 AWG stranded copper to the electrical ground rod. Unplugs antennas during electrical storms, and notes Joe K6AWA (at a more exposed, elevated location) needs more protection than most.

field.name: content
field.p: Found "Power, Grounding, Bonding, and Audio for Ham Radio" to be an excellent resource on lightning strikes and bonding technique. Looking to split a bulk purchase of grounding wire, since pricing varies a lot between suppliers.

field.name: content
field.p: The National Electrical Code requires #4 or #6 AWG minimum for electrical grounds - #8 wire won't be code compliant. Suggests checking Platt for competitive pricing on materials.

record.field: Local Powerpole standard configuration for 13.8V connections

field.name: content
field.p: What's the local SCRA standard Powerpole configuration for DC power connections to a mobile transceiver?

record.field: Local Powerpole standard configuration for 13.8V connections

field.name: content
field.p: We use the ARES standard configuration locally. Pre-bonded connectors are recommended to make sure they're assembled correctly - same configuration applies to accessories like inline meters.

record.field: Local Powerpole standard configuration for 13.8V connections

field.name: content
field.p: (Originally posted by Fred AE6SF on August 9, 2016)

The standard is "Red Right, Tongue Top." Anderson Powerpole connectors (PP15, PP30, PP45) are used for 12VDC systems - black is negative, red is positive. Contact size depends on wire gauge: PP15 for 18-16 AWG, PP30 for 14-12 AWG, PP45 for 10 AWG. Crimping is preferred over soldering, though cyanoacrylate glue works to bond the housings together.

Pelican cases turned out to be pricey, so I went looking for alternatives. Settled on a case made by Fuerte and sold by seahorsecases.com - made in the USA, meets Mil-Spec standards, lifetime guarantee, and about a third cheaper than Pelican.
The popular Pelican 1450 runs $94 on Google; the equivalent Seahorse SE-520 with padding is $48. For the KX3, I got the SE-430 model with padding - looks like it'll work out nicely.

field.p: (Originally posted by KI6UGB / Phil on June 5, 2017)
When learning Morse Code, pangrams (sentences using all 26 letters of the alphabet) are handy for practicing sending and receiving. The classic one: "The quick brown fox jumps over a lazy dog."
A few more, by character count:

ul.li: (31) The five boxing wizards jump quickly.
(32) Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs.
(35) The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
(41) A large fawn jumped quickly over white zinc boxes.
(44) Five or six big jet planes zoomed quickly by the tower.
(47) My grandfather picks up quartz and valuable onyx jewels.
(48) Fred specialized in the job of making very quaint wax toys.
(48) Sixty zippers were quickly picked from the woven jute bag.
(49) A quick movement of the enemy will jeopardize six gunboats.
(49) All questions asked by five watch experts amazed the judge.
(49) How razorback jumping frogs can level six piqued gymnasts.
(50) We promptly judged antique ivory buckles for the next prize.
